uncited: Planar Factorization methods represent continuous volumetric or spatiotemporal fields by decomposing high-dimensional feature tensors into a set of lower-dimensional 2D planes .
This approach solves the memory and computational bottlenecks of dense 3D/4D voxel grids and the black-box nature of pure MLP fields by using explicit, learnable planar structures .

Unlike sibling methods that aggregate features via concatenation or summation, this family typically employs element-wise multiplication (Hadamard product) of plane features to achieve spatial localization, enabling efficient decoding .
All methods in this family define a scene function $F_\Theta: \mathbb{R}^d \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^k$ using a set of parameterized 2D feature planes .
The input is a continuous coordinate vector $\mathbf{q} \in \mathbb{R}^d$ (typically spatial $\mathbf{x}$, viewing direction $\mathbf{d}$, or time $t$) .
The core mechanism involves projecting the $d$-dimensional query point onto $k = \binom{d}{2}$ orthogonal 2D planes .
For each plane $c$, features are retrieved via interpolation (bilinear or trilinear) from the plane grid $\mathbf{P}_c$ .
These features are then combined, typically via element-wise multiplication (Hadamard product) $\mathbf{f}(\mathbf{q}) = \prod_{c \in C} \mathbf{f}_c(\mathbf{q})$, to form a fused feature vector .
This product operation ensures that the resulting feature is non-zero only if the point lies within the active regions of all constituent planes, providing spatial localization .
The fused features are then decoded into density and color, either via a linear decoder with a learned basis or a small MLP .
Planar factorization emerged as a solution to the high memory costs of 3D/4D neural fields.
K-planes introduced the concept of factorizing 3D/4D fields into 2D planes using Hadamard products to enable linear decoding .
Forplane adapted this for dynamic surgical scenes, separating static and dynamic components .
Feature Grid as Radiance Field applied tensor factorization to spherical grids for egocentric views .
